title: Raga Sorath
hook: the Granth praises Sorath, but only on one condition

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Vadhans: wedding songs and songs of mourning in one raga, and your line was the same raga for both. Did you reach someone at a beginning, and someone at an ending? Day one thousand eighty-two.

A compliment with a condition attached. That's how the Guru Granth Sahib talks about today's raga. Somewhere inside the long Var of Sorath, between its stanzas, sits a short salok that names the raga itself and praises it. Sorath, it says, is always lovely. Then comes the word if. Not lovely because of its notes, or its singer, or the hour it's sung. Lovely if something is true of the person singing it. A raga that the book itself holds to a standard. Today: Raga Sorath, and what the condition is.
screen: `A COMPLIMENT WITH A CONDITION.` → `SORATH IS ALWAYS LOVELY…` → `…IF.`

segments.voice: First, where we are. The ragas of the Granth come in a fixed order, and we've been walking through them two days at a time. Sorath follows Vadhans. Its pages hold hymns by several of the Gurus and by Bhagats whose words the Gurus set beside their own, and then a Var, a ballad of stanzas with saloks between them. Tradition links Sorath with steady faith. Teachers describe the moods of ragas in different ways, so hold that as tradition, not as a rule written in the Granth. Now the salok. In paraphrase: Sorath is always lovely if the true one dwells in the mind. It goes on with plain pictures of a clean mouth and an honest tongue, a person whose speech and heart match. Notice what the verse is doing. A raga is a mood made of sound. You could sing Sorath perfectly, every note in place, and by this verse's measure it wouldn't yet be lovely. The beauty is finished by the one who sings it, by what lives in the mind while the mouth makes music. So where does steady faith come in? A mood that only lasts as long as the song isn't steady. The salok asks for something that stays put when the music stops: the true one held in the mind, always. Sorath sada suhavani, always lovely, is a big promise for a tune. The verse makes it a promise about a person instead. That's the line for today. Steady faith.
screen: `SORATH FOLLOWS VADHANS IN THE BOOK.` · `HYMNS, BHAGATS, AND A VAR.` · `LOVELY IF THE TRUE ONE DWELLS IN THE MIND.` · `THE SINGER FINISHES THE SONG.` · then, large: `STEADY FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Sorath, and keep one thing steady. If you can, play a recording of a shabad sung in Raga Sorath; searching for Sorath kirtan will find one. If not, sit in the quiet. Either way, choose one steady thing to rest on: the breath at the tip of the nose, or a single word. When the mind wanders, come back without scolding. The music can rise and fall around you; the one thing stays. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the word you return to. If you don't, the breath is enough. The bell holds the time.
Raga Sorath. The raga that follows Vadhans, which tradition links with steady faith, and which the Granth calls always lovely, if the true one dwells in the mind. Today's word.
Your line: steady faith. Once today, while doing something ordinary, a dish, a commute, a reply, check whether your words and your mind are saying the same thing. Day one thousand eighty-two.

howItsDone: In kirtan, ragis sing shabads from the Sorath section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Sorath, and the Var of Sorath, with its saloks between stanzas, is also sung or read in the sangat.
